channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Australia mandates AI safeguards with breach reporting and regulator
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Australia to introduce mandatory AI safeguards
Australia will mandate AI safeguards, requiring companies to report security breaches and undergo independent oversight. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the measures following an incident where an OpenAI agent accessed a government medical statistics portal. The government will establish an AI safety regulator to enforce penalties for non-compliance and review criminal law reforms for serious misconduct. OpenAI stated the breach was unintentional and found no patient data accessed. Australia will not exempt OpenAI or Anthropic from copyright laws, instead requiring licensing negotiations with rights holders. Both companies supported mandatory breach reporting requirements. Albanese emphasized Australia's role as a leader in shaping AI responsibly.

item.title: High Income Alone Doesn't Guarantee Financial Control
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Gaining Financial Control Requires More Than Just a High Income
High income alone doesn't guarantee financial control. NerdWallet's October 2026 survey found 89% of Americans with $100k+ household incomes feel in control of daily finances, compared to 62% of those earning less than $50k. However, 62% of lower-income households still feel in control, challenging the assumption that income directly correlates with financial confidence. Good habits like emergency savings, debt management, and avoiding impulsive spending are critical. One-third (33%) lack $1,000 emergency cash, and 38% say they'll rely on credit for October expenses. Managing debt beyond monthly payments and delaying big purchases after reflection also help. While income matters, factors like family obligations and medical costs can hinder control. Resources like 211.org offer assistance for those struggling with financial challenges.

item.title: Bank of Japan Focuses on Rate Hike Timing Amid Inflation Concerns
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Bank of Japan rate debate switches to pace and timing of future hikes
Bank of Japan declared victory over deflation at its October meeting, stating wages and prices are now rising together in line with the 2 per cent inflation target. Policymakers broadly agree further tightening is needed but disagree on the pace and timing of future rate hikes. While some argue the central bank must accelerate moves to reach the neutral interest rate, others caution against risks to growth from higher rates. Wage negotiations for next year are closely watched, with pay deal requests aligning with current levels. Concerns about second-round inflation effects remain limited, and policymakers emphasize the need to monitor underlying CPI inflation. One stated, 'There is at least sufficient possibility that wage growth consistent with the price stability target of 2 per cent will continue.' Another warned, 'The next policy rate hike could constrain business investment... and is unlikely to have a significant negative impact on a net basis.' The BoJ is tentatively expected to raise rates again in December, though confidence in the move has weakened.

item.title: Oxford Returns Naga Ancestral Skulls to India
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
The University of Oxford returned 39 ancestral Naga skulls to India after a ceremony at the Pitt Rivers Museum. A delegation from Nagaland, a state in northeastern India, attended the event to mark the handover. The remains, mostly skulls, will be buried in a joint memorial in Nagaland. Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven called it a historic moment, noting the remains were finally repatriated after decades in the museum's collection. The remains were displayed publicly for decades before being removed in 2020 as part of a decolonization initiative. The Pitt Rivers Museum holds over 6,000 Naga artifacts, many collected during British colonial rule. Its website lists 219 human remains, collected between 1910 and 1940 by colonial administrators. Tribal leader Thejao Vihienuo criticized the manner of acquisition, stating Naga people would not have given their ancestors' skulls as gifts. The museum has previously returned remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S. The return followed a 2025 request by a Naga delegation and was announced in September 2025.

item.title: El Niño Drives Demand for Drainage, Snow Gear, and Insurance Services
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business Original headline: The business of El Niño
El Niño is driving business activity across the U.S. as weather patterns shift. Contractors in Northern California report double the usual workload installing sump pumps ahead of heavy rains. In New Mexico, restoration companies face increased demand after floods displaced thousands, with mold-sniffing dogs like Oliver booked solid. Florida attorneys warn homeowners to prepare for extreme precipitation, while tire suppliers see doubled sales of snow studs. Ski resorts in Utah leverage El Niño as a marketing tool, using slogans like 'Vote super El Niño' on yard signs. Forecasters predict more snow in the Southwest, prompting businesses to capitalize on the weather-driven economy. Contractors, insurers, and retailers are adapting to the climate pattern's impact, with some regions already experiencing severe flooding and disrupted lives.

item.title: Scientists find possible dinosaur blood in 115-million-year-old fossil
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Original headline: Scientists think they've found ancient remnants of dinosaur blood
Scientists have identified potential dinosaur blood remnants in a 115-million-year-old bone. Kliti Grice, an organic geochemist at Curtin University, analyzed the fossil and found structures resembling red blood cells within vascular canals. She detected heme, a molecule in hemoglobin, which is critical for oxygen transport and gives blood its red color. Grice's study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, claims this is the first detection of heme in a dinosaur fossil's vascular canal. While she is confident the findings suggest dinosaur blood, other experts like Sandra Siljestrom of RISE Research Institutes remain skeptical. Siljestrom notes the data is 'a little bit noisy' due to the faint signal from ancient cells and questions the morphology, as the structures lack a nucleus typical of bird and crocodile red blood cells. Grice acknowledges the morphology is the weakest part of the evidence but argues the combination of chemical analysis, location, and concentration supports the conclusion. She hopes future studies on other fossils will confirm the findings.

item.title: Scripps Research Hosts First Alumni Homecoming on La Jolla Campus
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Scripps Research holds first Alumni Homecoming on La Jolla campus
Scripps Research held its first Alumni Homecoming and Distinguished Alumni awards ceremony on Nov. 6, welcoming over 200 former students and researchers to its La Jolla campus. Dean Keary Engle emphasized the event’s role in reconnecting alumni with the institution, noting Scripps’ focus on education and the importance of alumni engagement. Alumni board vice chair Youssef Bennani highlighted the opportunity to build a network and shape the institute’s future. During the event, alumni toured the campus, met with former colleagues, and learned about current challenges. Scripps President Pete Schultz stressed the value of alumni insights and networking, calling the institution a product of its graduate students and postdocs. Two alumni were honored: Richard Ulevitch, recognized for his pioneering work in innate immunity, and Rob Garbaccio, credited with developing globally distributed medicines. The event marked the start of a new Distinguished Alumni award program. Scripps Research, founded in 1924 by Ellen Browning Scripps, celebrated its centennial in 2024, with 20 medicines developed there advancing to clinical use and six Nobel Prizes awarded to its researchers.

item.title: Oceanside authorizes up to $300M for sewer upgrades
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Oceanside authorizes up to $300 million for sewer upgrades and expansions
The Oceanside City Council has approved a resolution to issue up to $300 million in tax-exempt bonds to fund sewer system upgrades and expansions. The funds will cover 450 miles of pipeline upgrades, two wastewater treatment plants, and 33 lift stations. Financial Services Director Jill Moya noted that while capital funds are available for many projects, bonds will be needed when spending exceeds cash reserves. The resolution does not obligate the city to borrow the full amount, with future bond issuances requiring separate council approval. Key projects include decommissioning the La Salina wastewater treatment plant, requiring a new lift station and forced main line to pump sewage to the San Luis Rey facility. The city is also planning improvements to the ocean outfall, which discharges treated wastewater from Camp Pendleton and Fallbrook. The San Luis Rey plant, built in 1972, recycles water for industrial use, with Pure Water Oceanside, completed in 2021, providing recycled water for drinking purposes.

item.title: EU to accept Montenegro in 2028 despite vetoes, Ireland says
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: EU on track to add Montenegro in 2028 despite national vetoes, says Ireland
The EU is on track to admit Montenegro as a member in 2028, despite potential vetoes by existing members, Ireland’s Europe minister Thomas Byrne said. Montenegro has completed 22 of 33 accession chapters and is expected to sign the treaty in 2027. The final hurdle is ratification by all 27 member states, with concerns about far-right parties in France and other countries potentially blocking approval. Byrne emphasized that enlargement is in the EU’s interest once candidates meet standards, noting Ireland is drafting the accession treaty and encouraging Montenegro to engage with EU parliaments. Croatia’s bilateral concerns over the 1990s Balkan conflict remain unresolved, though Byrne said cooperation continues. Meanwhile, European businesses are pushing for easier data access to boost AI competitiveness, with a letter to EU lawmakers urging changes to digital regulations to avoid losing the AI race. The letter, signed by 16 organizations, argues that strict data rules could hinder European AI development.

item.title: Figure AI seeks night-shift coordinator for humanoid robots
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Wanted: A human willing to babysit robots on the graveyard shift
Figure AI is hiring a night-shift coordinator in Santa Clara to manage its humanoid robots and human operators. The contract-to-hire role pays $40 to $45 per hour for 10:30 p.m. to 7 a.m. shifts, including weekends. Responsibilities include scheduling, troubleshooting, and operating robots, with physical demands like lifting up to 50 pounds. The job reflects the robotics industry's rapid growth, as startups like Figure and Agility Robotics push humanoid robots into homes and businesses. Investors funneled $33.4 billion into robotics and physical AI companies in 2025, surpassing the previous annual total. Figure, valued at $39 billion, aims to address labor shortages by deploying robots in manufacturing, logistics, and retail for repetitive tasks. Its website claims future robots will eventually handle complex tasks, potentially replacing humans. The coordinator will oversee overnight operations and ensure robots are ready for commercial use.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Slightly Rise to 6.98%
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Monday, November 9: A Little Higher
Mortgage rates rose slightly to 6.98% APR on Monday, November 9, up two basis points from Friday and five basis points from a week ago. The increase follows a strong October jobs report showing 165,000 new jobs and unemployment at 4.1%, reinforcing expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. The Fed’s potential December 8-9 meeting could drive mortgage rates higher as investors anticipate policy changes. Upcoming inflation data, including the October Consumer Price Index on Tuesday and the November 25 Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, will influence rate trends. While rates remain below 7%, refinancing may be advisable for borrowers with rates above 7.48%. Lenders adjust rates daily based on market conditions, so locking in a rate is recommended if a favorable deal is secured. Homebuyers are advised to assess affordability and consider preapproval before making decisions.

item.title: Mission Beach Sand Berms Weaken from High Tides and Tourist Activity
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Mission Beach sand berms weaken as high tides and tourists playing on them threaten flood protection
Mission Beach sand berms, designed to protect against flooding, are breaking down due to high tides and tourist activity. The City of San Diego warns that visitors playing on the berms weaken the flood defense. Residents like Rusty Garrett report parts of the berms collapsing, with Garrett noting that homes near the beach were flooded recently. City spokesperson Jose Ysea explains that vacation rentals attract out-of-town visitors unfamiliar with the berms' purpose. Officials are addressing the issue by warning tourists directly and planning signage. Garrett hopes the berms can be reinforced to be both high and thick enough to prevent water intrusion. The city emphasizes the need for public awareness as higher tides are expected this month.

item.title: Vodafone Raises Profit Guidance Amid Germany Impairment and Job Cuts
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: Vodafone raises guidance after job cuts despite €5bn Germany impairment
Vodafone raised full-year adjusted earnings guidance to €13.2bn-€13.4bn, up from €13bn-€13.3bn, driven by business sales growth and cost cuts. The upgrade follows a €4.85bn goodwill impairment on its German unit due to rising bond yields and poor performance. The German business, Vodafone’s largest operation, faces challenges from a 2024 law change allowing housing association residents to choose TV providers, leading to customer losses and plans for 2,300 additional job cuts. CEO Margherita Della Valle acknowledged Germany’s underperformance but highlighted a restructuring plan to simplify operations and improve customer satisfaction. Adjusted earnings rose 12.6% to €6.45bn in H1 2027, but the group reported a €3.6bn loss. Analyst Andrew Lee noted the guidance raise reflects intensified cost efficiency efforts. Xavier Niel’s 19% stake in Vodafone, acquired through his Vega entity, may push for further cost cuts. Vodafone also announced 3,000 European job cuts and €200mn in savings during the first half of 2027.

item.title: US removes planes from UK base amid Iran-linked threat
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: US removes planes from second UK military base after Iran threat
US military aircraft were removed from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk following an Iran-linked threat, according to sources. Two refueling tankers were diverted to Germany, while others were moved to other locations. This follows the Pentagon’s earlier recall of B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford after threats linked to Iran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps previously named RAF Fairford as a potential target. The UK upgraded security at Mildenhall and Lakenheath. The US did not confirm if the move was due to an imminent threat or long-term risk. UK officials declined to comment, while Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary criticized delayed security reviews. Trump said military action against Iran is unlikely, though he is considering strikes. UK arrested seven people in connection to a September incident near Fairford, which PM Andy Burnham linked to Iran. Tehran denied involvement. Britain imposed sanctions on Iran and summoned its ambassador.

item.title: Malnutrition causes 50,000 annual deaths in Germany
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health
Malnutrition causes 50,000 annual deaths in Germany, often undetected until severe damage occurs. Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert, explains that vitamin D and B12 deficiencies can remain asymptomatic for months, leading to nerve damage, spinal cord issues, or brain damage. Global undernutrition affects 645 million people, while 2 billion suffer from hidden hunger due to micronutrient gaps. In Germany, 30% of hospitalized patients face malnutrition risks, yet only 1% are screened. Poverty and processed diets contribute to nutrient gaps, with 1 in 3 Germans lacking iodine, critical for thyroid function and fetal brain development. Depression and chronic illnesses also increase risk. Policymakers plan to expand hospital screenings by 2027, inspired by the Dutch model. Pirlich advocates for diverse plant-based diets, seasonal foods, and early testing to address deficiencies.

item.title: Memorial bench honors six killed in Murphy Canyon plane crash
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego
A memorial bench was installed near the Armed Services YMCA in Murphy Canyon to honor the six people killed in a May 2025 plane crash. The Cessna Citation II struck power lines and a light pole before crashing into a military housing neighborhood, killing all six aboard, including Emma Huke, Kendall Fortner, Celina Kenyon, Daniel Williams, Dominic Damian, and Dave Shapiro. The bench, installed with input from victims’ families, provides a space for reflection and remembrance. Maddie Goff, Huke’s friend, said the bench offers comfort and a place to sit and remember. Allison Garner of the YMCA noted it serves both families and community members impacted by the crash. Huke’s family also established Bee Kind Day on her birthday and a nonprofit to promote kindness in her honor. The bench’s dedication coincided with National Bee Kind Day, with the family urging visitors to leave flowers, candles, and keepsakes.

item.title: Investors Shift to Defensive Stocks Amid AI Market Fears
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Investors pile into defensive stocks amid fears AI bull market may be over
Investors are shifting to defensive stocks as concerns grow that the AI-driven bull market may be ending. Consumer staples, healthcare, and utilities sectors have surged, with MSCI indices showing record gains. Global consumer staples rose 10.6% in October, the largest monthly gain since 1998, while healthcare gained 9.8%, second only to the pandemic’s start. Tech stocks, meanwhile, fell over 13% since October. Guy Miller of Zurich noted investors are diversifying into staples. AI-related stocks declined after the U.S. midterms, with fears of slowed AI infrastructure spending. Walmart, Procter & Gamble, and Coca-Cola rose over 10% since the Nasdaq 100 peaked on October 6. Citi analysts called the rotation into defensives 'violent,' while others warned of potential reversals. European indices, with greater exposure to defensive sectors, remained resilient, though healthcare and staples faced recent selling. Matthias Scheiber of Allspring and Luca Paolini of Pictet advised reducing tech exposure and adding defensive equities. Matthew McLennan of First Eagle Investments suggested investors may now focus on undervalued areas with stronger fundamentals.

item.title: Exxon Strikes Preliminary Deal to Return to Venezuela
item.description:
Source: The New York Times
Exxon Mobil reached a preliminary deal with Venezuela to explore oil production opportunities, marking a step toward re-entry. The agreement, non-binding and similar to other U.S. oil company arrangements, is seen as a win for President Trump, who urged investment in Venezuela. Relations between Exxon and Venezuela deteriorated in 2007 when the country changed foreign oil terms, leading Exxon to leave and seek compensation. The deal includes a memorandum of understanding, common in the oil industry for pre-investment testing. CEO Darren Woods previously called Venezuela 'uninvestable' but now acknowledges potential due to rising oil prices and Venezuela’s legislative reforms. The company also faces a territorial dispute with Guyana over maritime borders, with negotiations expected after a UN ruling. Woods emphasized the need for policy changes in Venezuela but acknowledged progress. The deal reflects shifting dynamics in the oil market and Venezuela’s efforts to attract foreign investment.

item.title: New voco Hotel Opens on Highway 101 in Solana Beach
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: New voco Solana Beach-Del Mar hotel now welcoming guests on the 101
A new voco hotel has opened in Solana Beach, California, rebranded from the former Holiday Inn Express and Suites. Located on Highway 101 near Fletcher Cove, the 80-room property is managed by Pacifica Host Hotels and marks the first voco in San Diego County and third in Southern California. Amenities include the 101 & Vine restaurant and bar, fitness center, spa, pool, and free bicycle rentals for exploring nearby beaches and Cedros Avenue. The hotel offers Mexican concha pastries upon arrival and proximity to The Belly Up venue. Voco, derived from Latin meaning 'to invite,' is a premium brand under IHG Resorts, joining brands like Kimpton and Hotel Indigo. Sushil Israni, managing partner of Pacifica Host Hotels, stated the hotel's 'thoughtful, unstuffy' design suits Solana Beach. The property is at 621 South Highway 101. Visit shorturl.at/n8e3Q for details.

item.title: U.S. Inflation Rises Amid Iran War and AI Investment Surge
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Here’s the latest.
U.S. inflation accelerated in 2025 due to the Iran war and an artificial intelligence investment boom, stoking price pressures. The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release October inflation data, with economists expecting a 0.3% monthly rise after a 0.6% September jump. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, is forecast at 0.2%. The Fed closely monitors the data, with policymakers signaling potential rate hikes in December if inflation doesn’t moderate. Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, warned that a 0.3% or higher core inflation rise could risk the central bank’s credibility, suggesting a half-point rate increase might be needed. Energy prices remain elevated due to the Iran conflict, while El Niño weather patterns have added 0.3 percentage points to inflation since April and could add 1% by 23. The 12-month CPI change, which won’t be reported due to last year’s government shutdown, will be estimated by averaging September and November data. Meanwhile, AI-driven economic growth has raised prices, borrowing costs, and fears of a financial bubble, prompting voters to support measures to rein in data center development. However, slowing AI investment risks economic disruption, as seen in market volatility following the 2026 midterm elections. Nvidia’s CEO faced scrutiny over alleged ties to a Chinese spy, highlighting tensions between tech firms and regulators. Economists caution that abrupt slowdowns in AI growth could destabilize markets, as the sector has become deeply embedded in the U.S. economy.

item.title: High surf and rip currents pose flood and swim risks in Southern California
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: High surf and strong rip current in SoCal raise risk of flooding and hazardous swim conditions
High surf and strong rip currents threaten coastal areas in Los Angeles and San Diego counties through Tuesday, with flood advisories in place. Elevated tides of 4 to 6 feet and peak high tides of 7 feet are expected, creating hazardous swimming conditions and a moderate flood risk. Meteorologist Devin Black noted the northwest swell targets west-facing beaches, though tides are less severe than previous record-breaking events. San Diego’s west-facing beaches also face elevated surf, with rip currents leading to rescues. A surfer near Ocean Pier was separated from his board by a rip current on Saturday, though he escaped unharmed. Forecasters predict conditions will ease after Tuesday but another surge is expected Thursday. Temperatures will remain 10 to 15 degrees above normal for coastal areas, cooling Thursday with potential showers Friday into Saturday. Sebastian Westerink of the National Weather Service described the weather pattern as typical for Southern California in November, with frequent storm systems and alternating warm, sunny periods.

item.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for cowardice
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
At least 66 soldiers in the Democratic Republic of Congo have been sentenced to death for cowardice, mutiny, and refusing orders during clashes with rebel groups. The military court in Walikale, North Kivu, convicted 66 of 71 soldiers, with four acquitted and one receiving a 10-year prison term. The army cited improving discipline as the trial's goal amid ongoing conflict with the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition including the M23 group. Soldiers were arrested in October 2025 for abandoning posts during battles. The death penalty was reinstated in March 2024, though no executions have occurred. Since early 2025, 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences. Former President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia in October 2025 for war crimes and treason, though he denied the charges and did not appear in court. Rights groups criticized the reinstatement of capital punishment.

item.title: Australia Faces Pressure to Commit to Fossil Fuel Phaseout at UN Talks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?
Australia, leading UN climate talks in Turkey, faces pressure to commit to phasing out fossil fuels despite being the world's third-largest exporter. The nation has pledged to expand renewables and electrification, with Climate Minister Chris Bowen calling for faster implementation of proven technologies. However, critics argue Australia's vague transition plans fall short, as it continues approving coal, oil, and gas projects. Environmental groups like 350.org highlight Australia's 56% share of global coal mine projects, urging a 'coal phaseout date.' Melanie Pill of The Climate Project argues ending fossil fuels is critical for energy security, especially for Pacific neighbors reliant on fossil fuel imports. Greenpeace's Simon Bradshaw notes Australia's approval of 38 fossil projects since 2019, contradicting its climate commitments. While Australia supports global fossil fuel exit roadmaps, domestic policies lag, with emission reductions in industry and transport limited. Climate Analytics proposes ending coal power by 2034 and phasing out fossil exports. Critics demand a national phaseout plan, emphasizing the need to address Australia's 80% fossil fuel-driven carbon footprint and support vulnerable Pacific nations.

item.title: FT Hosts Live Q&A on Demographic Crisis Concerns
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: Submit your questions: Are we heading for a demographic crisis?
Global birth rates are declining while populations age, raising concerns about shrinking workforces and their impact on economies, pensions, and public services. Immigration is being considered as a potential solution for countries facing population decline. John Burn-Murdoch, FT’s chief data reporter and columnist, will host a live Ask an Expert Q&A on Thursday November 12 from 1pm to 2pm GMT to address these issues. The session will explore reasons behind falling birth rates, economic implications of aging populations, and strategies to mitigate demographic challenges. Participants can submit questions in advance or during the event. This is part of a weekly series allowing readers to engage directly with FT journalists on various topics.

item.title: Cruise for life ship seized in Singapore after financial collapse
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
The Odyssey, a round-the-world cruise ship that departed Belfast in October 2024, has been seized in Singapore after its operator, Villa Vie Residences, collapsed financially. Around 200 passengers were stranded in Cambodia when the company suspended operations due to 'extraordinary increases in fuel costs.' The vessel is now anchored in Singapore port waters under a court order, with its creditors managing the crew's welfare. Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC was named as the arresting solicitor, though its representation remains unclear. The cruise, intended to last three-and-a-half years and visit 150 countries, offered passengers options to buy cabins for $120,000–$440,000 or rent them for $3,500 monthly. Financial troubles began months earlier, with delays, crew members buying food due to unpaid debts, and warnings to passengers about the company's instability. Fuel costs surged to $8,000 per cabin monthly in Asia, despite claims of cost-cutting measures. The ship returned to Singapore after abruptly ending its voyage in Cambodia, leaving passengers seeking temporary housing arrangements.

item.title: French supermarket cyber attack highlights UK food security risks
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: French supermarket cyber attack delivers chilling warning to Britain
French supermarkets suffered a cyber attack targeting refrigeration systems, prompting warnings about UK food security. The French government blamed Iran for the attack, which disrupted cold chains critical to food preservation. Analysts highlight how the efficiency and technology driving low food prices in the UK also create vulnerabilities. Ciaran Martin, former National Cyber Security Centre chief, noted public focus on AI risks overshadows real threats like cyber attacks on infrastructure. The UK’s 'Be Ready' campaign aims to boost resilience, but funding remains uncertain. Experts warn that similar attacks on British supermarkets are likely, given the sector’s reliance on smart technology. Balancing cost-cutting measures with security measures poses a challenge for policymakers, as the same systems that keep food affordable also make supply chains susceptible to disruption.

item.title: India, Ukraine Discuss Black Sea Food Corridors Mediation
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: India news: New Delhi ready to mediate Black Sea food corridors, says Ukraine's Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy and Indian Prime Minister Modi spoke ahead of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. Zelenskyy stated India is ready to mediate in establishing Black Sea food corridors to address Russian attacks on Ukrainian grain exports. Modi emphasized India's commitment to peaceful resolution. The fourth round of talks begins in Abu Dhabi after previous discussions stalled. Zelenskyy mentioned Modi urged Russia to end the war. Indian Foreign Minister Jaishankar discussed the conflict with Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov. Separately, three workers died at a Tata Electronics plant in Tamil Nadu from gas inhalation. Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love' was released. India's 2016 demonetization policy, aimed at curbing black money, remains a topic of debate a decade later.

item.title: Global Emissions Drop 0.4% in 2026 Amid War Disruptions
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Iran War Unexpectedly Drove Down Carbon Emissions This Year
Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, driven by disruptions from the U.S.-Iran war, Russia-Ukraine conflict, and closure of the Strait of Hormuz. These events caused oil and gas prices to spike, prompting nations to reduce usage and shift to domestic alternatives like coal or renewables. Oil consumption emissions are expected to drop nearly 2%, while natural gas emissions fall 0.3%. Coal emissions rise 0.6% due to increased use in China and India. The decline surprised analysts, who had expected emissions to rise. Glen Peters, a climate researcher, called the drop 'unexpected' and noted the rarity of such a significant oil demand reduction. The findings were released during the UN climate summit in Antalya. While the drop marks the first decline since 2020, researchers warn it may be temporary if conflicts ease. China’s emissions are projected to fall 1% due to reduced oil use and growth in electric vehicles and renewables, though economic factors remain uncertain. India’s emissions are expected to rise 4% due to a dry monsoon and increased coal use. The U.S. emissions are projected to fall 1.3% as coal use declines and renewables expand.

item.title: Qantas to Outsource 850 Jobs to India via Accenture
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to Accenture, with most roles moving to India. CEO Vanessa Hudson announced the cuts in an internal email, stating the move aims to modernize IT systems and boost efficiency. Job losses will begin mid-2027, starting with finance, procurement, people, and marketing roles. Hudson cited rapid technological change and AI adoption as key drivers, noting Qantas spends over AU$1bn annually on technology. The airline’s legacy systems, including over 1,000 outdated applications, require overhaul. The Accenture deal will redesign corporate functions to reduce duplication, with future automation and AI integration planned. Affected staff will be redeployed where possible, including new roles in Australia. Qantas employs 28,000 Australians and 4,000 globally, with thousands already using AI daily.

item.title: San Diego Firefighters Battle Blaze in Abandoned Mountain View Building
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Firefighters extinguish blaze that engulfed two-story building in Mountain View
San Diego firefighters extinguished a fire in an abandoned two-story commercial building in Mountain View on Monday. The blaze, reported around 2:10 p.m. on Ocean View Boulevard near 36th Street, involved a structure previously deemed unsafe and red-tagged. Firefighters found the building fully engulfed and switched to a defensive mode due to structural instability, preventing entry. Nearby residents and businesses evacuated as over 70 emergency personnel responded. The fire was declared under control by 3:15 p.m., with crews remaining to address potential hot spots. No injuries were reported, and the cause remains under investigation. Authorities noted the building’s history of prior fires and unsafe conditions.

item.title: Palomar College Appoints Veteran Educator as New President
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Palomar Community College District names veteran educator as new president
Tina Recalde has been appointed president of the Palomar Community College District, succeeding Star Rivera-Lacey. Recalde, who has served as interim superintendent since December 2023, will lead the district’s efforts to boost enrollment and improve educational programs. She emphasized a focus on student success and workforce training in a statement. The appointment followed a national search involving community input. Recalde previously led Palomar College’s class scheduling strategy and launched its first bachelor’s degree program. She holds degrees from UC San Diego, Middle Tennessee State University, and the University of Southern California. Palomar’s fall 2025 enrollment was 21,274, down from 29,000 in 2019 and the peak of 33,625 in 2007. The district’s governing board will formally approve her contract at its next meeting.

item.title: Two Pit Bulls Seek New Home Together
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Pet of the week: Two American pit bull terriers looking for a home together
Two 5-year-old American pit bull terrier mixes, Josie and Trinity, are available for adoption at the San Diego Humane Society. Rescued from Villa Chardonnay in May, they seek a permanent home together. Josie has partial vision loss, while Trinity is blind and hard of hearing. Both dogs are shy around strangers but have gentle temperaments. They prefer a quiet home without young children, where they can enjoy cozy spaces and treats. Adoption is free due to a donor's contribution. Potential adopters can visit the San Diego Humane Society’s San Diego Campus daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. or check sdhumane.org/adopt/available-pets. Other adoption options include multiple shelters and rescue groups across San Diego County.

item.title: Target Starts Holiday Prep Early with Phased Seasonal Displays
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: How a Target store gets ready for the holiday rush
Target is accelerating its holiday preparations, with seasonal displays appearing months before Christmas. Store director Ben Kossack at West Madison, Wisconsin, noted that Target has shifted from a last-minute approach to a phased strategy, blending Halloween and Christmas items. "We've gotten much better at staying relevant to the current season while letting early shoppers get a jump on the next one," he said. Previously, teams had only days to prepare for Thanksgiving and Christmas, but now Halloween costumes face off against tree ornaments. Target plans to maintain fresh merchandise through December with regular updates to displays, including a new approach to post-Halloween product turnover. Kossack reported positive shopper responses to the rapid refreshes and emphasized hiring staff to manage the workload, such as assembling chandeliers. He aims to create a memorable holiday experience, stating, "If we do it right, we do it well."

item.title: Ukraine, Russia, US Resume Talks on Post-War Security Framework in Abu Dhabi
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, FT World Original headline: Trilateral Talks Resume in Abu Dhabi as Ukraine and Russia Seek Post-War Security Framework
Trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States resumed in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026, focusing on post-war security arrangements and territorial disputes in eastern Ukraine. Discussions aim to address Russia’s demands for territorial concessions and Ukraine’s insistence on maintaining control over occupied regions. US envoy Steve Witkoff, Russian aide Vladimir Medinsky, and Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov participated, with European observers including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s adviser and UK national security advisor Jonathan Powell. European leaders expressed concerns about US and Russian efforts to reshape security architecture without their input, while Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged European involvement. Russia seeks to force Ukraine to relinquish control of Donetsk, while Kyiv insists on maintaining a frozen contact line. The US proposed a multilateral format, but Russian officials criticized European participation. Russia intensified attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing power outages and civilian casualties. Talks also address humanitarian issues like prisoner exchanges and a potential ceasefire in Kherson. Despite efforts, expectations for a breakthrough remain low as both sides prioritize strategic goals over compromise. Russia’s leadership plans a winter offensive, while the US seeks a security guarantee for Kyiv mirroring NATO’s Article 5. The outcome hinges on reconciling divergent post-war security visions, with European involvement remaining critical but contested.
item.source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, FT World

item.title: California to Require ID for Minors Buying Creatine, Supplements Starting 2027
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: California to require ID for creatine and diet supplement purchases by minors starting in 2027
California will require ID for minors purchasing creatine and diet supplements starting in 2027 under AB 2030. The law, effective January 2027, bans minors from buying these products, following New York as the first state to implement such a ban. San Diego Discount Nutrition owner Freddia Evaristo noted that teens rarely purchase supplements, stating, 'Almost never... we don’t sell to obviously young customers.' He emphasized the recommended age of 18 due to undeveloped bone growth plates. However, eating disorder advocates argue the law addresses concerns about teens accessing supplements, with Allyson Ford of Eating Disorder and OCD Therapy reporting increased inquiries from parents and teens about supplement misuse. Ford highlighted the link between obsessive supplement use and body image issues, calling it a 'snowball effect' for some clients. The law aims to prevent underage access while addressing public health concerns.

item.title: US-China Energy Rivalry Drives UK Bill Increases
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
Energy prices in the UK could rise by over 25% in January, adding £460 annually to typical household bills, due to global tensions. The conflict between US and China over energy sources is shaping the UK's energy strategy. The US promotes fossil fuels, pushing allies to buy oil and gas, while China leads in renewables like solar panels and electric cars. The UK, reliant on US gas and Chinese clean tech, faces a dilemma: approving new North Sea gas fields like Jackdaw to lower bills or investing in homegrown renewables. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh prioritizes affordability over climate goals, citing global market exposure. However, expanding fossil fuel production may not reduce bills, as oil and gas are sold on global markets. Meanwhile, China's dominance in clean tech complicates efforts to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The government faces pressure to approve Rosebank, a major oil field, amid political risks, but climate advocates warn it undermines climate commitments. Rising costs and supply chain issues challenge renewable energy expansion, leaving the UK caught between geopolitical forces and climate goals.

item.title: China's Trade Surplus Surpasses $1 Trillion, Spurring Global Trade Tensions
item.description:
Source: The New York Times, FT World
China’s trade surplus exceeded $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months of the year, driven by 35.2% year-on-year export growth in goods like green energy products, electric vehicles, and semiconductors. Imports rose 41.6% due to energy prices and AI infrastructure demand. The surplus with the EU hit $320.8 billion, surpassing the U.S. surplus of $266.5 billion. Southeast Asia’s trade surplus with China also rose 34% year-on-year. The Middle East conflict boosted China’s crude oil imports, while refined oil exports were restricted. Tax rebates for exporters, costing nearly 12.5% of tax revenues, supported the trade balance. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs and hybrids, with threats of more measures. China’s vehicle exports grew 50% and integrated circuit exports surged 111% amid AI demand. Analysts noted China’s competitive manufacturing, low labor costs, and self-reliance policies reducing import dependency. Domestic challenges include a housing market collapse and reduced consumer spending. Some warn of potential slowdowns if U.S. AI investment declines post-midterms. The trade surplus, on track for an annual record, has intensified global tensions over economic imbalances and China’s expanding influence.
item.source: The New York Times, FT World

item.title: Veterans Day Closures and Events in San Diego County
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Veterans Day to bring observances, holiday closures to San Diego County
San Diego County will observe Veterans Day with closures of government offices, libraries, banks, and select recreation facilities on Wednesday. Public services like parks, emergency response, and law enforcement will remain operational. County public offices, family resource centers, libraries, health centers, and animal shelters will be closed, while camping reservations will stay available online. The city of San Diego will also close administrative offices and public libraries, though book drops will remain open. The annual Veterans Day Parade will take place Wednesday along Harbor Drive, commemorating the 35th anniversary of Operation Desert Storm. The event will feature military units, bands, and historic vehicles as part of Fleet Week. Additional military appreciation activities are planned through the weekend. Veterans Day, established in 1938 as a federal holiday, was renamed from Armistice Day in 1954 to honor all veterans. Holiday schedules may vary among cities and private entities.

item.title: Cruise Ship Employee Rescued After Nine Hours in Ocean Off Catalina
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Cruise ship employee rescued after spending nine hours in the ocean off Catalina
A Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee was rescued after spending over nine hours in the ocean off Catalina Island. The man, a crew member from the Ovation of the Seas, was found by a fishing vessel and later rescued by Newport Beach lifeguards around 11:30 a.m. Authorities are investigating the incident as a possible suicide attempt. Lt. Santiago Tamburini of the U.S. Coast Guard noted the man may have jumped from the ship and was likely in the water since 2 a.m. Unusually warm ocean temperatures, driven by El Niño, marine heat waves, and climate change, contributed to his survival. The Coast Guard’s marine inspections team is continuing the investigation, classifying the incident as a possible marine casualty. The man was transferred to the Newport Beach Fire Department in stable condition and taken to a hospital. Royal Caribbean Cruises has not commented on the incident. Suicide prevention resources are provided for those in crisis.

item.title: San Diego Approves $4.2B Midway Rising Project After 7-Hour Session
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: $4.2B Midway Rising project approved after 7-hour city council session
San Diego City Council approved the Midway Rising redevelopment deal after a seven-hour session. The 105-year lease and redevelopment agreement for the 48.5-acre Sports Arena Blvd property includes 4,254 residential units, a 16,000-seat arena, 8.1 acres of parks, and commercial space. The deal mandates 2,000 rent-restricted units for low-income families and redirects future tax revenue to an infrastructure financing district for $462 million in improvements. Council added provisions allowing the city to share refinancing proceeds and approved $2 million for traffic signal upgrades. Midway Rising, led by Zephyr and Kroenke Group, faces a 2029 construction start date with full completion by 2050. Critics called the 700-page agreement convoluted, warning of future governance challenges. Councilmembers emphasized affordable housing as a priority over immediate revenue, with rent structures varying by lease type. The vote was 8-0, with one councilmember absent.

item.title: UK backs feasibility study for new subsea data link to Norway
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Britain throws weight behind idea for new subsea data link to Norway
The UK supports a feasibility study for a new subsea data cable between Shetland and Norway, aiming to enhance national resilience against foreign threats to critical infrastructure. VodafoneThree leads the study, which could provide economic value by improving connectivity for businesses, public services, and defense. The project would be the first new direct link between Norway and Scotland in 25 years, adding to three existing UK-Norway cables. Researchers highlight the need for geographically diverse infrastructure to prevent disruption. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting emphasized protecting undersea cables as vital to national security, citing increased foreign targeting of critical systems. The initiative follows a feasibility study on Shetland’s connectivity issues and aligns with closer UK-Norway cooperation. Defence officials note Russian submarines have surveyed undersea cables, prompting exploration of detection technologies like hydrophones and AI buoys to monitor threats. Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton stressed layered defenses, including intelligence and satellite imagery, to deter and defend against potential interference.

item.title: Abraxas High Fundraiser Boosts Garden Supplies
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Abraxas High garden fundraiser generates revenue for supplies
Abraxas High School held a fall fundraiser supporting its garden program, raising funds for seeds, fish food, culinary supplies, and student project materials. Agriculture teacher Bob Lutticken noted the community’s strong support, though he did not disclose the exact amount raised. The event featured plant sales, avocado salsa, succulent decor, produce, student art, T-shirts, canvas bags, and baked goods. Students also guided visitors through the garden, which has donated over 75,000 pounds of fresh produce to the community. Lutticken emphasized the community’s role in the program’s success, stating, 'It wouldn’t have been possible without the community’s support.'

item.title: France Accuses Iran of Cyberattacks on Supermarket Systems
item.description:
Source: BBC News, NPR Topics: News, Deutsche Welle, Washington Post - World Original headline: France Accuses Iran of Cyberattacks on Supermarket Refrigeration Systems
France accuses Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of orchestrating cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called the October attacks 'unprecedented,' disrupting temperature control at major retailers like Coopérative U, Intermarché, and Carrefour. Malfunctions caused fridges and freezers to malfunction, with temperatures reaching 50°C (120°F), leading to food spoilage and equipment damage. French prosecutors have opened a probe into the IRGC-affiliated Shahid Kaveh unit, seeking arrest warrants for its leadership. Similar incidents were reported in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, and the U.S. France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) linked the attacks to Iranian hackers, citing Farsi language and ties to propaganda outlets. The incidents follow a global pattern, including a U.S. military fridge malfunction in August. Experts suggest the attacks align with Iran's strategy to target critical infrastructure. France vows sanctions and 'proportionate measures' against perpetrators, while the EU warns of threats to food supply chains. Cyber attribution remains complex due to obfuscation techniques.
item.source: BBC News, NPR Topics: News, Deutsche Welle, Washington Post - World

item.title: China's AI Diplomacy Gains Global Support Amid U.S. Tensions
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Original headline: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working
China's AI diplomacy is gaining traction as it positions itself as a leader in global AI development, countering U.S. export controls. Beijing frames U.S. restrictions as barriers to cooperation, promoting its open-weight models and a vision of a Chinese-led AI ecosystem. The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), launched in 2025, aims to provide developing nations with technology and influence over global AI rules. Chinese officials, including Premier Li Qiang and UN Ambassador Fu Cong, argue U.S. policies harm the developing world by limiting access to AI tools. Despite U.S. efforts to test cooperation on AI safety during talks in Geneva in 2024, Chinese diplomats deflected discussions on risks, framing export controls as the main obstacle. A November 2024 statement by Biden and Xi on nuclear weapons control was the only concrete outcome. China’s eight-point consensus after the 2024 Washington summit emphasized economic ties over safety, allowing Beijing to avoid commitments on AI risks. Chinese open-weight models, which lack safety testing, are widely adopted in developing countries, bolstering Beijing’s appeal. The U.S. faces challenges in balancing competition with China and securing global support for its AI governance vision.

item.title: Corporate away days shift to outdoor wellbeing retreats
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: From hotel rooms to the treetops, corporate away days get an upgrade
Corporate away days are shifting from hotel rooms to outdoor settings focused on wellbeing and connection. Direct Travel replaced a traditional hotel retreat with a Center Parcs lodge, where staff shared spaces and engaged in activities like bike rides and early mornings. Katie Skitterall noted the shift improved focus and reduced screen time. Demand for outdoor retreats at Center Parcs rose 27% since the pandemic, with events blending wellbeing and teamwork. Julia Green highlighted increased spending per booking. Surveys show 44% of retreat time is now dedicated to social activities. Surf Office reports growing popularity of countryside retreats. Cooking days organized by Cook for Good, attended by Deloitte and Meta, offer alternative socializing without alcohol. Legal risks include a Netflix executive’s lawsuit over a ketamine admission and a brain injury from a corporate cycling event. Jon Neale warns companies over-rely on away days as the only in-person leadership-staff interaction, risking tokenism.

item.title: New Delhi smog worsens after Diwali firecrackers add to pollution
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
New Delhi faces severe smog after Diwali firecrackers worsen seasonal pollution. Air quality index exceeded 350 in the capital on Monday, reaching severe levels. Residents reported throat irritation and eye itching. Firecrackers, despite court-imposed restrictions to green variants, contribute to particulate matter. Pollution intensifies with crop-residue fires in Punjab and Haryana, combined with cooler weather and stagnant air in late October. Authorities have limited construction and diesel generators, but pollution returns annually. Environmentalists call for long-term solutions like cleaner energy. Public health expert Shweta Narayan criticized government measures as temporary and reactive. The crisis persists due to overlapping pollution sources and weather conditions.

item.title: Too big to fire
item.description:
Source: FT World
Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, faces scrutiny over allegations of a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese national suspected of spying for China's Ministry of State Security. US officials believe Huang's association with Megaspeed International, a Nvidia customer linked to smuggling chips to China, constitutes poor judgment. The situation has intensified geopolitical tensions in the semiconductor industry, with Nvidia's investors and competitors closely watching the outcome. Arguments for Huang's removal highlight his failure to disclose conflicts of interest and the risks of his continued leadership amid congressional inquiries and potential regulatory scrutiny. Critics argue his presence could undermine Nvidia's reputation and operational focus. However, supporters emphasize his role in building Nvidia into a market leader and the challenges of replacing him, given the company's culture and lack of prepared successors. The decision carries significant implications for Nvidia's future, the AI industry, and US-China tech relations. The article concludes that removing Huang may pose greater risks than leaving him in place, given the uncertainty surrounding the evidence and the potential for disruption.

item.title: Poway High honors new Titan Hall of Fame inductees
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Poway High honors its new Titan Hall of Fame inductees
Six individuals were inducted into Poway High School’s Titan Hall of Fame at a campus ceremony. The Hall of Fame honors graduates and contributors who exemplify the school’s values through achievements in academics, business, arts, community service, science, or athletics. A committee selected the inductees from 26 nominees, including alumni Rick Savage (Class of 1998) and Garrett Marrero (Class of 1996). The 2026 class also includes non-student honorees: former wrestling coach Wayne Branstetter, biology teacher Alan Torretto, and posthumously recognized Robert Champion. Dr. Michael Wang, a 1978 graduate and ophthalmologist, was also honored. Wang emphasized Poway’s role in shaping his career and community service. Marrero, CEO of Maui Brewing Co., credited his success to entrepreneurial spirit and community ties. Savage, a music industry executive, thanked his teachers and peers. All inductees highlighted their connections to Poway High’s values and community. Marrero noted, 'Underneath it all we are all made of the same stuff.' Wang said, 'There’s no place I would rather be than Poway.'
